w: Nearly eighteen kilometres of manuscript shelving alone, inside the library that quietly runs Trove - the service that has put millions of digitised Australian newspapers, photos and documents online for free. Created by Act of Parliament in 1960, it is the country's biggest library by any measure.
s: Eighteen kilometres of shelving, one Act of Parliament.
_facts: Largest reference library in Australia, created by the National Library Act 1960
By June 2019 its collection held 7,717,579 items, with manuscripts occupying 17,950 metres of shelving
Hosts and manages Trove, including the Australian Web Archive and National edeposit, and digitised newspapers/documents/images

w: One dish here, DSS-43, is the only antenna on Earth that can send a command to Voyager 2 - a spacecraft now further from home than anything else humans have built. The complex has been listening to the solar system since 1965, when it tracked the Apollo Lunar Module for NASA.
s: The only antenna on Earth that reaches Voyager 2.
_facts: Satellite communication station at Tidbinbilla, ACT, part of NASA JPL's Deep Space Network, opened 1965
Used for tracking the Apollo Lunar Module; sister stations at Goldstone, California and Madrid, Spain
Its DSS-43 antenna is the only one on Earth able to send commands to Voyager 2
Managed in Australia by CSIRO for NASA's Space Communications and Navigation program

w: Australia's oldest telescope stood here until the 2003 bushfires tore through and destroyed it along with several others on the mountaintop. Now part of the Australian National University's astronomy school, the observatory rebuilt and kept watching the southern sky regardless.
s: The 2003 bushfire took the oldest telescope in Australia.
_facts: Observatory west of Canberra, part of the ANU Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics
Australia's oldest telescope, and several others, destroyed by bushfire in 2003

w: Drive up General Bridges Drive and you're looking down on the Australian Defence Force Academy and Duntroon's parade grounds from 663 metres up. The summit carries a memorial to every rank of the Royal Regiment of Australian Artillery - a gunners' lookout, open daylight hours only.
s: A gunners' memorial with the Academy at your feet.
_facts: Hill, elevation 663 metres, in the north-eastern suburbs of Canberra
Overlooks the Australian Defence Force Academy and the Royal Military College at Duntroon
Summit carries a memorial to all ranks of the Royal Regiment of Australian Artillery
Accessible by car via General Bridges Drive, open to the public during daylight hours

w: More than 166,000 works under one roof, from a gallery the federal government only got around to founding in 1967 - late, for a country with this much art already worth collecting. It has since made up the ground, becoming one of Australia's largest public art museums.
_facts: National art museum of Australia, one of the largest art museums in the country, holding over 166,000 works
Established 1967 by the Australian Government as a national public art museum

w: Built into the hill itself rather than on top of it, so the public can walk over the roof of their own Parliament - the whole point of the 1988 design. It replaced the old building down the road after sixty years, cost over a billion dollars, and was opened by the Queen herself.
s: A Parliament you can walk over the roof of.
_facts: Meeting place of the Parliament of Australia, on Capital Hill, designed by Mitchell/Giurgola & Thorp Architects
Replaced Old Parliament House, where Federal Parliament sat 1927-1988
Officially opened 9 May 1988 by Elizabeth II; cost more than $1.1 billion

w: Phar Lap's actual heart sits in the same collection as the first prototype Holden ever built - fifty thousand years of Indigenous heritage under one roof alongside the literal organs of a national obsession. It didn't get a permanent building on Acton Peninsula until 2001, worth the wait.
s: Phar Lap's heart and the first Holden, side by side.
_facts: National public museum on Acton Peninsula, established by the National Museum of Australia Act 1980
Profiles 50,000 years of Indigenous heritage, settlement since 1788, and Federation
Holds the world's largest collection of Aboriginal bark paintings and stone tools, plus the heart of racehorse Phar Lap and the Holden prototype No. 1 car
Did not get a permanent home until 11 March 2001

w: Eight hundred and twelve metres of native bushland rising straight out of the north shore of Lake Burley Griffin, close enough to the city centre to see it from the CBD. Protected as Canberra Nature Park, it stays wildlife habitat rather than becoming another lookout car park.
s: Wild bushland minutes from the CBD.
_facts: Mountain, elevation 812 metres, west of the Canberra CBD, on the northern shore of Lake Burley Griffin
Protected by Canberra Nature Park, covered in native bushland, a haven for native wildlife

w: Only native Australian flora gets a place here - the largest living collection of it anywhere, assembled since 1949 on the slopes below Black Mountain. Federally run and heritage-listed since 2004, its herbarium code CANB shows up in botanical citations worldwide.
s: The country's biggest native-only plant collection.
_facts: Heritage-listed botanical garden in Acton, established 1949, administered by the federal government
Added to the Commonwealth Heritage List 22 June 2004
Largest living collection of native Australian flora; herbarium code CANB

w: At 890 metres, this is the highest point inside Canberra's urban boundary - just pipping its far more famous neighbour, Mount Ainslie. Folded into the Canberra Nature Park, it draws a fraction of the visitors Ainslie's lookout does, despite outranking it by every measure that counts.
_facts: Mountain, elevation 890 metres, in the northern suburbs of Canberra
Close to Mount Ainslie; the highest point within Canberra's urban boundaries
Contained within Canberra Nature Park

w: Fifty-four hectares of parkland wrapped around the residence where the Governor-General signs off on the business of government, invests Australia's honours, and receives foreign heads of state. The monarch uses it too, on the rare occasions Canberra gets a royal visit.
_facts: Official residence of the Governor-General of Australia, in the suburb of Yarralumla
Main residence set amid 54 hectares of parkland, added to Commonwealth Heritage List 2004
Governor-General presides over Federal Executive Council meetings, holds investitures, and receives heads of state and ambassadors' credentials
Also used by the Monarch of Australia when in Canberra

w: The seat of the Archbishop of Canberra and Goulburn stands not in the suburb its name suggests, but in Manuka - officially part of Forrest, practically the capital's most walkable village centre. The city's Catholic centre of gravity, quietly overshadowed by the monuments up the hill.
s: The capital's Catholic seat, tucked into Manuka.
_facts: Main Roman Catholic place of worship and seat of the Archbishop of the Archdiocese of Canberra and Goulburn
Located in the suburb of Forrest, in the local centre known as Manuka
